passages.title: The Inevitable Event shatters the world
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat open the surah by announcing one thing and then describing it from every side: the arrival of the Day of Resurrection. Ayat 1–3 name the Event and settle its certainty and its consequence; ayat 4–6 show what it does to the solid world we stand on. Read the renderings in sequence and you notice that the passage keeps saying *when* — "When the Waqi'ah occurs… When the earth will be shaken" — and only at ayah 7 does it turn to us: "And you (all) will be in three groups."

## The surah that turned the Prophet's hair grey

Before the words themselves, the sources give us a scene. Abu Ishaq reported from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Abu Bakr said, "O Allah's Messenger! You are becoming grey?" He ﷺ replied:

> "Hud (chapter 11), Al-Waqi'ah (56), Al-Mursalat (77), 'Amma Yatasa'alun (78) and Idha Ash-Shamsu Kuwwirat (81) have made me grey."

At-Tirmidhi collected this hadith and said, "Hasan Gharib."

Al-Waqi'ah is on that list. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself named it among the surahs whose weight showed on him visibly. If our reading of ayat 1–6 leaves us unmoved, the problem is not with the verses.

## Ibn Mas'ud on his deathbed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a second scene, which Ibn Kathir cites on the authority of Ibn 'Asakir from Abu Zabyah. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud lay dying, and 'Uthman came to visit him.

"What are you suffering from?" — "From my sins."

"Do you desire anything?" — "Yes, Allah's mercy."

"Shall I call a doctor for you?" — "It is the doctor who has given me the ailment."

"May I send you an allowance from the public treasury?" — "I have no need for it."

"Accept it, please. You are leaving daughters behind you. It will help them."

And Ibn Mas'ud answered: "You are worried about my daughters that they must not suffer from poverty. I have no such worry, because I have instructed them to recite Surah Al-Waqi'ah every night. I have heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, *'Whoever recites Surah Al-Waqi'ah every night will never suffer from poverty.'*"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir, after citing this story from Ibn 'Asakir, supported it with other chains of transmitters and other sources.

Notice the logic of a man who has genuinely absorbed this surah: a father on his deathbed, offered state money for his daughters, declines it — because he has already left them something he considers better security. The surah that describes the world being pulverised is, for him, the surah that removes anxiety about provision.

## Ayah 1: naming the Day "The Event"

**إِذَا وَقَعَتِ ٱلۡوَاقِعَةُ — "When the Inevitable Event takes place."**

Ibn Kathir explains that *Al-Waqi'ah* — "the occurrence" — is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection, "because that Day is real and will surely come." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān echoes him: it is called Al-Waqi'ah because there is no room for doubt in its occurrence; it is real and will surely come to pass.

Sit with that for a moment. The Day is not named after its terrors, or its judgement, or its fire. It is named after the plain fact that it *happens*. Ibn Kathir points to the same name used elsewhere: "Then on that Day shall the Waqi'ah occur" (69:15).

## Ayah 2: nothing will deny it

**لَيۡسَ لِوَقۡعَتِهَا كَاذِبَةٌ — "then no one can deny it has come."**

Everything turns on the word *kādhibah*, and the sources give two readings, both worth holding.

**First**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *kādhibah* here is the verbal noun, like *'āfiyah* and *'āqibah* — that is, a word that looks like a participle but functions as an abstract noun. On this reading the sense is: **the news of the occurrence of this event cannot be false news.** Every other report you have ever received might turn out to be wrong. This one cannot.

**Second**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some authorities take *kādhibah* in the sense of *takdhīb*, "to deny" — and then the meaning is clear: **no one can deny the fact that it will come to pass.** In this life denial is easy and cheap. On that Day the Event will be far too overwhelming to argue with.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a statement about power: when Allah commands the Day of Resurrection to begin, **none can stop it from happening or prevent it from beginning.** He brings a chain of supporting verses:

- "Answer the call of your Lord before there comes from Allah a Day which can not be averted." (42:47)
- "A questioner asked concerning a torment about to occur — upon the disbelievers, which none can avert." (70:1–2)
- "And on the Day He will say: 'Be!' — and it is! His Word is the Truth. His will be the dominion on the Day when the Trumpet will be blown. All-Knower of the unseen and the seen. He is the All-Wise, Well Aware." (6:73)

Two early authorities are quoted directly on this word. Muhammad bin Ka'b said simply: "It will certainly occur." Qatadah said: "It shall not be discontinued, taken back or aborted." That last phrase repays sitting with — no postponement, no reversal, no cancellation halfway through.

And notice what 42:47 quietly does to the reader. It converts certainty into urgency: *respond now, because the door does not stay open.*

## Ayah 3: the great reversal

**خَافِضَةٞ رَّافِعَةٌ — "It will debase some and elevate others."** Ibn Kathir's rendering is even barer: "Bringing low, exalting."

Two words, and the Event itself is what does the lowering and the raising. It does not merely reveal ranks; it *rearranges* them.

Ibn Kathir reports from Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others that this means Al-Waqi'ah "lowers some people to the lowest parts of the Fire, **even if they had been mighty in this life**. It also elevates others to the highest grades in the residence of eternal delight, **even if they were weak in this life**."

That double "even if" is the heart of the ayah. Every hierarchy you can see today — wealth, lineage, office, reputation — is provisional. The Day does not inherit our rankings; it overturns them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops the same theme from the worldly side, reporting it as Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation: the Event will bring about a great revolution in the lives of men, like the upheaval seen when governments are overturned — "the high and the mighty will be laid low and the despised and down-trodden will be exalted; the poor become rich and the rich become poor." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the purpose of putting it this way is to depict the horrors of the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir also preserves a second and quite different reading, reported by Al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: *khāfidah rāfi'ah* describes the **sound** of the Event — "It made the near and the far hear it." 'Ikrimah spelled it out: "It lowered, and thus those who were close heard it, and elevated, and thus those in the distance heard it." Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said similarly. On this reading the Event is a summons pitched so that no ear on earth can miss it — low enough for the near, high enough for the far.

The scholars genuinely differed here, and both meanings are transmitted from the earliest generations. The two words are spare enough to carry both.

## Ayat 4–6: the ground goes

Having established *that* it comes and *what* it does to people, the passage turns to what it does to the earth. Read ayat 4, 5 and 6 as one continuous demolition in three stages.

**Ayah 4 — إِذَا رُجَّتِ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ رَجّٗا, "when the earth will be violently shaken"** — or, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "shaken with a terrible shake." He glosses it: the earth "is shaken and moved violently over all of its surface and through its depths." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others said it means "Violently shaken."

Ar-Rabi' bin Anas gives the image that makes it concrete: **"The earth will be shaken with all that is in it, just as a sifter is shaken with its contents."** Not ground trembling beneath objects that stay put — the ground and everything on it tossed together, the way a sieve throws grain. Ibn Kathir links this to "When the earth is shaken with its earthquake" (99:1) and to the warning: "O mankind! Have Taqwa of your Lord! Verily, the earthquake of the Hour is a terrible thing" (22:1).

**Ayah 5 — وَبُسَّتِ ٱلۡجِبَالُ بَسّٗا, "and the mountains will be crushed to pieces"** — Ibn Kathir: "the mountains will be powdered to dust." He explains the sense as **"relentlessly pulverized,"** and reports that this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and others. Ibn Zayd said the mountains will become exactly what Allah described elsewhere: "a heap of sand poured out" (73:14) — a shape that cannot hold itself up, collapsing as fast as you pour it.

Why mountains? Because they are the standing picture of permanence. Whatever a person imagines is too big to move, this Day grinds down.

**Ayah 6 — فَكَانَتۡ هَبَآءٗ مُّنۢبَثّٗا, "becoming scattered particles of dust"** — Ibn Kathir renders it "so that they will become floating dust particles." The early authorities reached for four everyday images, all preserved by Ibn Kathir:

- 'Ali (narrated by Abu Ishaq from Al-Harith): "It will become like the rising dust storm that soon fades away leaving no trace of itself behind."
- Ibn 'Abbas (reported by Al-'Awfi): it "describes the rising embers from the fire when it is kindled, but when the embers land, they are extinguished quickly."
- 'Ikrimah: "The floating dust particles that the wind scatters all around."
- Qatadah: "Like the dry parts of trees that the wind scatters all about."

Every one of these has the same shape: something that rises impressively and is then simply *gone*, leaving nothing behind. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah is similar to several other ayat indicating that the mountains will be moved from their places, demolished and blown off their bases, becoming like carded wool on the Day of Resurrection.

Follow the sequence deliberately: solid earth (ayah 4) → pulverised rock (ayah 5) → drifting dust (ayah 6). In three short ayat the most stable thing you know is reduced to something the wind pushes around.

## Where the passage is heading

The passage does not stop here, and it was never meant to. Everything from ayah 1 to ayah 6 is scene-setting; ayah 7 turns from the world to us: "And you (all) will be in three groups."

So the demolition in ayat 4–6 is not the point of the passage. It is the clearing of the stage. Once the mountains are dust and every worldly ranking has been overturned by ayah 3, the only question left standing is which of the three groups you are in.

## Living it

**Stop investing in what ayah 3 will overturn.** The sources are blunt: worldly might will not survive that Day, and worldly weakness will not disqualify anyone from the highest grades. Any status that depends on other people recognising it is precisely the kind of status Al-Waqi'ah re-sorts.

**Take the urgency of 42:47 personally.** Ibn Kathir chose that verse to explain ayah 2, and it is a command, not a description: answer the call of your Lord *before* the Day that cannot be averted arrives. Certainty about the future is only useful if it changes the present.

**Let the four images of ayah 6 test what you are building.** A dust storm that fades leaving no trace; embers that die the moment they land; dust the wind scatters; dry leaves blown about. If mountains end that way, ask honestly which of your own projects are built to end that way too.

**And keep the surah close.** Ibn Mas'ud, offered money for his daughters, preferred to leave them the nightly recitation of Al-Waqi'ah. A surah about everything solid turning to dust turned out to be, for him, the answer to anxiety about provision — because once you truly know in Whose hand that Day lies, you know in Whose hand your sustenance lies too.

passages.title: Humanity divided into three groups
passages.tafsir:
After the world has been shaken apart in ayat 1–6 — the earth shaken violently through all its surface and depths, the mountains relentlessly pulverized until they are nothing but floating dust — these six ayat turn from the collapsing earth to us. What holds ayat 7–12 together is one act of sorting: humanity divided into exactly three groups, two of them named by the side they are taken to, and the third named not by a side at all but by how it lived.

## The sorting is what the Hour is *for*

Ayah 3 had already described that Day as **khāfiḍah rāfiʿah** — "bringing low, exalting." Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others explained that this Day "lowers some people to the lowest parts of the Fire, even if they had been mighty in this life," and "elevates others to the highest grades in the residence of eternal delight, even if they were weak in this life."

Ayat 7–12 are that sentence being filled in with names. Every ranking this world took seriously — the mighty, the well-placed, the overlooked — dissolves along with the mountains, and one new ranking replaces it. If you have been reading the surah asking "what is all this upheaval *for*?", ayah 7 answers: **it is for this division.**

## Three groups — and the address is to you

**وَكُنتُمْ أَزْوَاجًا ثَلَاثَةً** — "and you will be [divided into] three categories."

The address is plural and direct: *you*, all of you. Nobody is standing outside the count of three. And this is not offered as a possibility. The surah opened by declaring that there is no **kādhibah** regarding the occurrence of that Day — Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that when Allah commands the Day of Resurrection to begin, none can stop it from happening or prevent it from beginning. Muhammad bin Ka'b glossed the word simply: "It will certainly occur." Qatadah glossed it: "It shall not be discontinued, taken back or aborted."

Ibn Kathir sets out the three categories, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows him closely:

- **One group at the right of Allah's Throne** — those who were brought forth from the right side of Adam (peace be upon him). They will be given their Books of Records in their right hands and taken to the right side. They are the people of Paradise, and **As-Suddi** explained that they will make up the *majority* of Paradise's residents.
- **One group at the left of the Throne**, brought forth from Adam's left side, given their Books of Records in their left hands and taken to the left. They are the residents of the Fire — Ibn Kathir breaks off here to say *may Allah save us from their actions*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, *we seek refuge in Allah from their behaviour pattern.*
- **The foremost (As-Sābiqūn)**, who are the ones brought near (**Al-Muqarrabūn**). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says they will be placed **in front of** the Divine Throne. Ibn Kathir says they are "in a better grade and status and nearer to Allah than those on the right side" — indeed they are "the chiefs of those on the right side" — and that they are **fewer** than the people of the right.

Ibn Kathir links this threefold split to another ayah where Allah divides the recipients of His Book into three: "of them are some who wrong themselves, and of them are some who follow a middle course, and of them are some who are, by Allah's leave, foremost in good deeds" (35:32).

## Two named by a side, one named by a life

**فَأَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ** — "the people of the right, how blessed will they be!"
**وَأَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ** — "the people of the left, how miserable will they be!"

Each of these two ayat names a group, then says the name again — and stops. Ibn Kathir's rendering has to supply the missing word in brackets to make it land in English: "how **(fortunate)** will be those on the right… how **(unfortunate)** will be those on the left." The Qur'an does not describe them here. It gestures at something and leaves the space open. The fuller description is coming: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that towards the end of the surah the three categories are taken up again.

Notice too what these two groups are named by: **which side they are on.** The right and the left, and which hand holds the record. Then the third group breaks the pattern completely — it is named by an action.

**وَالسَّابِقُونَ السَّابِقُونَ** — the name is simply said twice. The other two groups needed an exclamation to hint at their fate; this one carries its own verdict in its own name. Ibn Kathir's explanation runs straight through it: "The meaning of foremost is that they were foremost in performing the acts of righteousness just as Allah commanded them." Foremost *here*, therefore foremost *there*.

## Who are the foremost?

The early scholars held a strikingly wide range of views about who the Sābiqūn are:

- **Mujahid** said they are **the Prophets** — and Ibn Kathir reports the same view from **Muhammad bin Ka'b** and **Abu Hazrah Ya'qub bin Mujahid**.
- **As-Suddi** said they are the residents of the utmost heights of Paradise (**Ahl al-ʿIlliyyīn**).
- **Ibn Sirin** said they are the early Muslims who prayed facing **both qiblahs** — Bayt al-Maqdis and Bayt Allah.
- **Al-Hasan and Qatadah** said that in **every Ummah** there are Sābiqūn — this is not a distinction reserved for one community.
- **Some commentators** said, quite plainly, that they are **the people who go first to the mosque**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Ibn Kathir cites all these views and concludes that **they are all correct in their own right and not in conflict with one another** — because the Sābiqūn are "those who must have been foremost in their invincible faith and righteous deeds in this world, and as such they would be the 'Foremost' in the Hereafter in terms of reward which will befit their faith and good deeds."

That conclusion is worth pausing over. The list runs from the Prophets down to the man who leaves the house early for the mosque, and the commentary does not treat that as a collapse from the sublime to the trivial. It is one quality showing itself at different scales: **getting there first.** Ibn Kathir grounds it in what Allah commanded for this life — "march forth in the way to forgiveness from your Lord, and for Paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth" (3:133), and "race with one another in hastening towards forgiveness from your Lord" (57:21) — and then states the principle: "the reward is according to the kind of deed, and as one does, so he is judged." Whoever races in this world is placed in the front rank in the next. The prize matches the running.

## What being first actually earns

**أُوْلَٰئِكَ الْمُقَرَّبُونَ — فِي جَنَّاتِ النَّعِيمِ** — "They are the ones nearest to Allah, in the Gardens of Bliss."

The reward is announced in two stages, and the order is worth noticing. First **nearness** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses Al-Muqarrabūn as the believers "who are granted special nearness to Allah." Only then the **Gardens of Delight**. Ibn Kathir's whole description of this group turns on that same word: they are "nearer to Allah than those on the right side." The people of the right are the people of Paradise and its majority; the Muqarrabūn are the few who are brought close.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists who they include: **the Messengers, the Prophets, the Ṣiddīqīn (the truthful), the martyrs, and the friends of Allah.** Ibn Kathir's list runs closely parallel: "the Messengers, Prophets, true believers and martyrs."

## From the Sunnah — who reaches the shade first

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings, at this ayah, a tradition recorded by **Imam Ahmad** on the authority of **ʿA'ishah** (may Allah be pleased with her). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked the Companions: *"Do you know who will be the first to be accommodated in the Divine Shade on the Day of Resurrection?"* They replied, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He ﷺ said they are:

1. **Those who accept the truth when it is presented to them.**
2. **Those who, when asked for the rights due from them, fulfil them.**
3. **Those who judge about the matters of others as they would judge about themselves.**

This is the most practical thing in the whole passage. Being among the first is not, here, a matter of spectacular worship. It is three ordinary, difficult habits: not arguing with the truth once you have seen it; paying what you owe — money, time, apology, obligation — when it is asked of you; and holding your own case to the same standard you hold everyone else's. Anyone can begin these today.

## Living it

**Read yourself into ayah 7.** The whole force of "and you will be three groups" is that it is addressed to you. The right, the left, the foremost — you are already in one of these. It is not decided at the end of time; it is being decided now, by whether you race or drift.

**Take the modest door.** The commentary accepts *both* that the Sābiqūn are the Prophets *and* that they are those who go first to the mosque. If the first door seems impossibly far above you, the second is open this evening. Being foremost is a habit of arriving early to what Allah has called you to — early to prayer, early to repentance, early to the good you have been putting off.

**Do not confuse ease here with rank there.** Al-Hasan and Qatadah's comment stands over this whole passage: the Day brings low those who were mighty in this world and raises those who were weak. The sorting of ayat 7–12 will overturn every arrangement you are currently impressed by, including your own place in it.

**And it starts earlier than you think.** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah divides people into these three groups **upon their death**, as the end of the surah indicates; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — signs begin to appear from the time of a person's death indicating which of the three categories he or she will fall into. The Day of Resurrection publishes the verdict; the death of each person delivers it.

It is worth remembering, finally, what Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) once said to the Prophet ﷺ — "O Allah's Messenger! You are becoming gray?" — and the answer he received: that Sūrah Hūd, **Al-Wāqiʿah**, Al-Mursalāt, ʿAmma Yatasā'alūn and Idhā ash-Shamsu Kuwwirat had made him gray. At-Tirmidhi collected this hadith and said, "Hasan Gharib." This surah weighed on the heart of the best of creation ﷺ. It is not meant to be read lightly.

passages.title: The foremost: their multitudes and their banquet
passages.tafsir:
Having named the third and highest class of people — **as-Sābiqūn**, the Foremost, who are "the nearest to Allah" in the Gardens of Delight (ayat 10–12) — Allah now tells us two things about them: **how many** they are and where they come from in history (ayat 13–14), and **what their life looks like** once they are seated there (ayat 15–21). The unit holds together as a single scene: first the guest list, then the banquet. Everything from ayah 15 onward is one continuous picture — thrones, company, servers, drink, fruit, meat — of people at rest and at ease, being served.

## Ayat 13–14: "A multitude from the earlier, and a few from the later"

**The word ثُلَّة (thullah).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *thullah* means "a party, group, company," and cites Zamakhshari that it refers to "a throng or a large number of people." So the contrast in ayat 13–14 is not subtle: a *crowd* from the earlier, a *few* from the later.

That single word set off one of the more interesting discussions in the tafsir literature — because "earlier" and "later" are not defined in the text.

**The two views.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out clearly.

*The first view:* "earlier generations" means all of Allah's creation from the time of Ādam up to just before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and "later generations" means all of it from his coming until the Day of Judgement. This is recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim with a chain from Mujahid and Hasan al-Basri, and it is the reading Ibn Jarir preferred; Bayān ul-Qurʼān also adopts it. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Jarir supported it with the Prophet's ﷺ words, "We are the later nation, but the foremost on the Day of Resurrection" — and that Ibn Jarir mentioned no other interpretation at all, nor attributed this one to anyone else.

*The second view:* "earlier" and "later" both refer to **this Ummah** — the earlier being the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and their pupils, whom a hadith terms *khayr al-qurūn*, "the best generation," and the "later" being everyone who came after them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Qurtubi, Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, Mazhari and others prefer this.

**Why the second view is preferred.** Ibn Kathir is blunt about it: Ibn Jarir's choice is "questionable, rather it is a deficient interpretation." His argument is from the Qur'an itself — this Ummah is the best of all nations by the text of the Qur'an, as in *"You are the best of nations"* (3:110). If that is so, it is not possible that the foremost believers of earlier nations outnumber the foremost of this Ummah; the opposite is true. So ayah 13 speaks of the **earlier** generations of this Ummah, and ayah 14 of its **later** generations, from whom only a small number will be counted among the Foremost.

Mazhari argues the same way and adds a second text: this Ummah's higher rank is proved by *"You are the best Ummah raised for the good of mankind"* (3:110) and *"so that you should be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger a witness to you."*

Ibn Kathir supports his reading with the early authorities. Ibn Abi Hatim records that as-Sarī ibn Yahya reported that al-Hasan al-Basri recited ayat 10–13 and then commented: "A multitude from the earlier generation of this Ummah." Ibn Abi Hatim also records Muhammad ibn Sīrīn saying of ayat 13–14 that they "stated, or hoped that they will all be from this Ummah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a Prophetic hadith on the same side, quoted from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī: Musaddad in his *Musnad*, Ibn ul-Mundhir, Tabarani and Ibn Marduyah report **with a good chain** from Abu Bakrah that the Prophet ﷺ, interpreting the two *thullah* mentioned in 56:39–40, said, "**They are both from this Ummah.**" Many scholars of hadith report a similar tradition **with a weak chain** from Ibn ʿAbbas, worded, "They are from my Ummah." If that is right, then ayah 7 of this surah, *"and you will be divided into three categories,"* is addressing the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and all three classes will be drawn from it.

**A note on honesty in the sources.** In support of the *first* view, Ibn ʿAsakir transmits with his chain a report from Jabir that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab asked, "O Messenger of Allah, will there be a larger number of the Foremost from among the earlier generations and a small number from amongst us?" — that for about a year no revelation came on the matter, and that when 56:39–40 came down the Prophet ﷺ called ʿUmar and said, "O ʿUmar, listen to what Allah has revealed… Behold! From Ādam to me is one *thullah*, and my Ummah is another *thullah*." Ibn Kathir quotes this report and records his own reservation about its chain: *"In its chain of transmission, there is some defect."* That is worth pausing on. Ibn Kathir passes on a report that supports the view he rejects, and says plainly what he thinks of its chain rather than quietly leaving it out; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, on the other side, marks the Ibn ʿAbbas wording as weak even though it favours the view it prefers. The weakness gets named whichever direction the report points.

## Why this ayah unsettled the Companions

Ibn Kathir records, from Ibn Abi Hatim on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that when ayat 13–14 were revealed "this news became hard for the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ" — they understood them to mean that the foremost believers of earlier nations would outnumber those of this Ummah. Then came 56:39–40, *"A multitude of those will be from the first ones, and a multitude of those will be from the later ones."* And the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "I hope that you will comprise a quarter of the residents of Paradise, a third of the residents of Paradise. Rather, you are a half of the residents of Paradise, and will have a share in the other half."

Imam Ahmad also recorded this; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the report from Imam Ahmad and Ibn Abi Hatim on the authority of Abu Hurayrah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then raises the obvious objection: ayah 40 relates to the **People of the Right**, while ayah 13 was about the **Foremost** — so how did ayah 40 remove the Companions' concern about ayah 13? Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī resolves it: the Companions in general, and ʿUmar in particular, were saddened by ayah 13 presumably because they assumed the proportion would carry over — that the later generations would be equally few among the People of the Right, and so their share of all the inmates of Paradise, put together, would be very small. Ayat 39–40 clarified exactly that: taken collectively, the **majority** of the inmates of Paradise will be the followers of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, even if the number of later generations among the Foremost is smaller compared to the previous nations — especially since a large number of those previous nations will comprise the **Prophets**. In relation to them, it does not matter if the followers of the Prophet ﷺ are fewer.

**The scale of this Ummah's share.** Both sources gather the reports:

- Imam Bukhari narrates from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, "Will it please you if you are a quarter of the inmates of Paradise?" The Companions said yes, and he said, "By Him in Whose control is my life! I hope that you will comprise a half of the inmates of Paradise."
- Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Darimi record from Bahz ibn Hakim: "You are complement to the seventy nations of the days of yore. You are the choicest one and the most honourable one in the sight of Allah."
- Tirmidhi, Hakim and Baihaqi record from Buraydah: "The inmates of Paradise will be ranged in 120 ranks: eighty of them will be from this Ummah, and forty from the rest of the nations." (Tirmidhi rated it *hasan*, Hakim *sahih*.)
- Ibn Kathir notes it is *mutawātir* — reported by so many routes that it is beyond doubt — that the Prophet ﷺ mentioned seventy thousand of this Ummah entering Paradise without reckoning; and in other narrations of the same hadith, "With each thousand, another seventy thousand," and "With every one of them is another seventy thousand."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the apparent inconsistency in the fractions — the ratio is given as a third, a quarter, a half and two-thirds at different times. There is no conflict: these were based on the estimation of the Prophet ﷺ, which had been increasing on different occasions.

Ibn Kathir also grounds the "earlier is better" principle: there is no doubt that the earlier generations of each nation were better than the later ones, and it is confirmed in the authentic hadith compilations, from more than one route, that he ﷺ said, "The best people are my generation, then the next generation, then the next generation." Yet he ﷺ also said, "A group of my Ummah will always remain on the truth and dominant, unharmed by those who fail to support them and those who defy them, until the Last Hour begins" — in another narration, "until Allah's command comes while they are like this." Ayah 14 says the later ones among the Foremost are *few*; it does not say they are *none*.

## Ayat 15–17: the seating, the company, the service

**"On thrones, mawḍūnah" (15).** Ibn ʿAbbas explained *mawḍūnah* as "woven with gold," and similar was reported from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds — citing Ibn ʿAbbas as recorded by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Baihaqi and others — that it means "fabric woven or inwrought with gold thread." The image is of a couch whose very fabric is threaded through with gold.

**"Reclining thereon, face to face" (16).** Ibn Kathir draws out the point: this indicates that they will face each other, and **none of them will be in the back lines**. In any worldly gathering someone is seated behind someone else, someone is at the edge of the circle. Here there is no edge. And reclining is the posture of a person at ease — the whole scene is one of rest.

**"Immortal boys will go around them" (17).** *Wildān mukhalladūn* — youths who, as Ibn Kathir says, "will never grow up, get old or change in shape." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the preferred opinion is that these youths of Paradise, like the fair damsels of Paradise, will have been born in Paradise. They will be the servants of the inmates of Paradise, and hadith narratives indicate there will be thousands of such servants for each of the inmates.

## Ayat 18–19: the drink, and what it is free of

**The vessels (18).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the three words apart: *akwāb* (plural of *kūb*) are cups or glasses used for drinking; *abārīq* (plural of *ibrīq*) are jugs with spouts; *kaʼs* is a wine glass. Ibn Kathir adds the finer distinction: these cups do not have handles or spouts, while the jugs sometimes do and sometimes do not.

The last word carries the weight: *min maʿīn*, from a **flowing spring**. Both sources note that the glasses contain wine drawn from a flowing spring — and Ibn Kathir presses the contrast: "not from containers that might get empty. Rather, this spring of wine flows freely." This drink is not rationed out of a store. The supply is not a cellar; it is a spring.

**What it does not do to them (19).** Two verbs, both denials.

*Lā yuṣaddaʿūn.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives it from *ṣudāʿ*, "headache": when worldly wine is taken in large quantity it gives the drinker excruciating headache and makes him feel dizzy, and the heavenly wine is free from such harmful effects. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfī, Qatadah and as-Suddi — "It does not give them a headache."

*Wa lā yunzifūn.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the verb to the root *nazf*, whose root meaning is "the well became empty, all the water having been taken out of it." Here, it says, it means "the spring of his brain or mind or senses became exhausted." That is the picture the word carries — a well drained dry — and the ayah denies it of them.

It is worth noticing that the two commentaries render the phrase slightly differently. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān translates it "nor will they be intoxicated," and Ibn Kathir glosses the pair together as "they will never get headaches from this wine nor intoxicated." The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites put it more precisely: "It does not change their sense of reasoning." One names the state that is absent; the other names the faculty that is preserved.

Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The wine (of this life) has four side-effects, it intoxicates, gives headaches, induces vomiting and causes excessive urine. So Allah mentioned the wine of Paradise free of these characteristics." Ibn Kathir's summary is the point of the ayah: this wine "does not affect their minds, even though it has a strong and tremendously delightful taste." The pleasure is kept; the harm is stripped out. Read that way, a believer who gives up an intoxicant in this world is not being told that pleasure itself is bad — he is being told to wait for the version of it that costs him nothing.

## Ayat 20–21: fruit they choose, and meat they desire

**"And fruit that they may choose" (20).** Ibn Kathir: "whatever fruits they wish for will be distributed among them." Note what the ayah names — not only the fruit, but the choosing.

Ibn Kathir draws a small, very human legal point from exactly that: this ayah "is a proof that we are allowed to choose the fruits that we prefer and wish to eat."

Under this ayah he records a dream narration — reported by Imam Ahmad from Thabit from Anas, and collected by Abu Yaʿla, of which al-Hafiz ad-Diyāʼ said, "This hadith meets the criteria of Muslim." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ liked dreams; if a man had a dream he would ask about him if he did not know him, and would like to hear the dream if that man was praised for his good qualities. A woman came and said she had dreamt she was taken out of Madinah and entered Paradise, and heard a noise because of which Paradise wept; she looked and found twelve men, whose names she mentioned — men the Prophet ﷺ had sent with a military expedition — brought in with their wounds still bleeding. It was said, "Take them to the river Baydakh," and they were taken to that river and submerged in it, and their faces turned as radiant as the full moon. They were brought a plate made of gold containing green dates, and they ate as much as they wanted, and whenever they turned that plate around they would eat from the fruit it then contained, as much as they wanted — and she ate with them. Later the army sent an emissary with the news, naming the very twelve men who had died. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the woman and asked her to tell her story again, and she did. The turning plate is ayah 20 in a picture: whatever they choose, already there.

**"And the flesh of fowls that they desire" (21).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes simply that it is recorded in a Prophetic Tradition that the inmates of Paradise will get the meat of whatever birds they desire, as and when they desire it.

Ibn Kathir gives a narration recorded by **Imam Ahmad** — and he notes that only Imam Ahmad collected this hadith using this chain of narration — from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Birds of Paradise are like Bukht camels that graze in the trees of Paradise." Abu Bakr commented, "O Allah's Messenger! Surely, these birds must be wonderful." The Messenger ﷺ said, "**Those who eat them are more wonderful**" — and repeated this statement three times. Then he went on, "And I hope that you will be among those who eat from them."

That exchange is worth sitting with. Abu Bakr's attention went to the bird; the Prophet ﷺ turned it back to the one who eats it. And he did not end with a description — he ended with a hope, spoken out loud, that his companion would be among them. That is the same voice that had earlier told the Companions, when ayat 13–14 fell hard on them, "I hope that you will comprise a quarter of the residents of Paradise… rather, you are a half." Ayah 14 says the later generations of the Foremost are few. It does not say none.

passages.title: Pure companions and pure speech for the foremost
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the long description of *al-sābiqūn* — the foremost, whom the passage calls the nearest to Allah. The verses move from what these servants of Allah are given to **whom they are with** (ayah 22), **what they are like** in their purity (ayah 23), **why any of it is theirs** (ayah 24), and finally **what their world sounds like** (ayat 25–26). The thread running through all five is purity: pure companions, an unmixed recompense, and speech with nothing ugly in it.

## A word of context

These ayat finish a sentence that began several verses earlier. From ayah 15 onward Allah furnishes a scene: thrones — *mawḍūnah*, which Ibn ʿAbbās glossed as "woven with gold" — on which they recline facing one another, with immortal youths circulating among them carrying cups and jugs and a glass of flowing wine. Ibn Kathir notes of that wine that it causes no headache and does not touch the mind, and he cites the report of aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās that the wine of this world has four side-effects, from all of which the wine of Paradise is free.

That is the logic our five ayat inherit: each delight is named, and its defect is removed. So when ayah 22 arrives, we are already trained to expect a pleasure without its shadow.

## Ayah 22 — the companions

**وَحُورٌ عِينٌ** — "and maidens with gorgeous eyes." Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "Ḥūr with wide lovely eyes."

Notice how little the Qur'an says here. After thrones, servants, wine, fruit and fowl described at length, the companions of Paradise are named in two words. Grammatically the phrase is simply joined by "and" to the list that came before — the same construction that brought them fruit and fowl now brings them companionship. The catalogue has been building from things to persons, and it lands on the human good last. Then, rather than lingering, the ayah moves straight into an image.

## Ayah 23 — like preserved pearls

**كَأَمْثَالِ اللُّؤْلُؤِ الْمَكْنُونِ** — "like pristine pearls." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line, and it is the key to the image: they are "just as white and pure fresh pearls."

Sit with the word *maknūn*, "preserved," "kept." A pearl that has been kept is a pearl nothing has got at. No handling has dulled it, no dust has settled on it. It is not simply beautiful; it is **unspoiled**.

That is a very different compliment from the ones this world hands out. The Qur'an does not praise these companions for being displayed; it praises them for being *guarded*. And it fits the passage exactly. The wine is pleasure without the headache; the pearl is beauty without the tarnish.

Having explained this simile, Ibn Kathir points the reader elsewhere for the fuller picture: he recalls Allah's words **كَأَنَّهُنَّ بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ**, "as if they were eggs preserved" (37:49) — the same root *maknūn* again, the same idea of a smooth, sheltered, untouched thing — which he treated in Sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt (chapter 37), and he notes that their description also comes in Sūrat ar-Raḥmān (chapter 55). The restraint here is itself instructive: the passage names a reality, gives one image for it, and declines to dwell.

## Ayah 24 — the whole scene, priced

**جَزَاءً بِمَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ** — "as a reward for what they used to do." Ibn Kathir explains: "these delights that We granted them are rewards for the good deeds that they performed" in this life.

Structurally this is the hinge of the passage. Everything from ayah 15 to ayah 23 has been a catalogue of gifts, and now a single word — *jazāʾ*, recompense — reaches back and attaches every item on that list to something a believer once did on earth. The gold-woven thrones, the drink that never clouds the mind, the pure companions: all of it is answer, not accident.

The Arabic verb is worth noticing. It is not simply "for what they did" but **كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ** — a form that reports sustained, habitual action: *what they used to do*, day after day, as a way of life. The reward is lasting because the deeds were not a stunt but a settled character.

## A brief note on who "they" are

Since ayah 24 rewards *them*, it is worth noting that the commentators genuinely differed over the identity of the foremost described earlier in the sūrah as "a multitude from the first ones and a few from the later ones."

Some, as reported from Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's collection, took "the first ones" to mean earlier believing nations and "the later ones" to mean this Ummah. Ibn Jarīr preferred this, supporting it with the Prophet's ﷺ words, "We are the later nation, but the foremost on the Day of Resurrection." (Ibn Kathir names no collection for that wording, so neither will we.)

Ibn Kathir considered that choice questionable and, in his words, a deficient interpretation, arguing from the Qur'an that this Ummah is the best of all nations, so the foremost of earlier nations cannot outnumber the foremost of this one. He preferred the other reading: that "a multitude from the first ones" means the **earlier generations of this Ummah**, and "a few from the later ones" its **later generations**. He cites al-Ḥasan, who on reciting the ayah commented, "A multitude from the earlier generation of this Ummah," and Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, who understood the foremost to be entirely from this Ummah — both reports in Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Since the earlier generations of every nation were better than their later ones, he adds, the ayah may in that sense take in the previous believing nations too.

There is mercy folded into this. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that when the ayah about "a few of those from the later ones" was revealed, this news became hard for the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. Then came the later ayat of this same sūrah: **a multitude from the first ones, and a multitude from the later ones.** And the Prophet ﷺ said, "I hope that you will comprise a quarter of the residents of Paradise, a third of the residents of Paradise. Rather, you are a half of the residents of Paradise, and will have a share in the other half." Imam Ahmad also recorded this.

## Ayat 25–26 — what Paradise sounds like

**لَا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيهَا لَغْوًا وَلَا تَأْثِيمًا** — "There they will never hear any idle or sinful talk." Ibn Kathir's summary is direct: they will not hear foul or unnecessary speech in Paradise. He brings the parallel from 88:11, where Allah says of the Garden that no harmful speech or falsehood is heard in it — meaning, he explains, that no foul words are uttered there.

Two different faults are ruled out, and it helps to keep them apart:

- **Laghw** is speech that is *unnecessary* — vain, pointless, going nowhere. It need not be wicked. It is simply noise: the conversational filler that fills an evening and leaves nothing behind.
- **Taʾthīm** is speech that carries *sin* in it. Ibn Kathir glosses it as speech containing foul words: the insult, the obscenity, the talk that makes speaker or hearer guilty.

Between them these two words cover almost everything that goes wrong with human company. Think honestly about how much of what we hear in a day is one or the other. Then notice what the ayah promises: **not a single instance**, ever, across an eternity of conversation. This is the last defect removed. The thrones were furnished, the drink was purified, the companions were preserved — and now the *atmosphere* is cleaned. A gathering can have every luxury in it and still be ruined by what people say.

Then ayah 26: **إِلَّا قِيلًا سَلَامًا سَلَامًا** — "only good and virtuous speech," literally, "except the saying: peace, peace."

The Arabic is an exception clause. Having excluded all idle and sinful speech, Allah carves out what remains — and what remains is *salām*. Ibn Kathir explains that they greet one another with *salām*, as Allah says elsewhere, "Their greeting therein will be: peace" (14:23), and he repeats that their words are free of impure and needless speech.

The doubling — *salāman salāman* — is not a stammer. It is the sound of a place where the greeting keeps passing from one person to another and back again, around a company all of whom are safe, none of whom says a word that could wound.

## Living it

This is a description of the next world, but it hands us one immediately practical thing. Of all the pleasures Allah names in these ayat — the drink, the fruit, the companions — the only one we can begin to imitate today is the last. We cannot manufacture the drink of Paradise. We can decide that our gatherings will hold no *laghw* and no *taʾthīm*, and that what passes between us is *salām*.

And ayah 24 tells us the connection is not decorative. That whole scene is *jazāʾ* — recompense for what people **used to do**, habitually, over a lifetime. Whoever trains their tongue now toward peace is not merely being pleasant; by Allah's grace they are doing the very kind of deed for which such a place is given.

**A note on how to hold all this.** Everything here — the thrones, the pearls, the pure companions, the greeting — is knowledge that reaches us only through revelation. We affirm it exactly as Allah and His Messenger ﷺ described it, without straining to picture the mechanics and without explaining it away into metaphor. Ibn Kathir's own method in this passage is the model: he says what the words mean, points to the parallel ayat, and stops.

passages.title: The people of the right: trees and spreading shade
passages.tafsir:
Having described the end of those foremost in faith, the nearest to Allah, the sūrah now turns to **the people of the right**. Ayah 27 asks who they are and what awaits them; ayat 28–30 begin the answer, and they begin it, remarkably, with two trees and a shadow.

## Ayah 27: a question that is really an exclamation

**"And the people of the right — how blessed will they be!"** In Arabic the phrase doubles back on itself: *wa aṣḥāb al-yamīn, mā aṣḥāb al-yamīn* — "and those on the right; how fortunate will be those on the right?" Ibn Kathir reads this as a genuine question posed in order to be answered: *who* are those on the right, what is their condition, and what will their final destination be like? Allah then answers it Himself in the ayat that follow. The effect is of a curtain drawn back slowly: the name is announced, the listener leans in, and only then is the scene described.

**Where they stand.** Ibn Kathir notes that after Allah mentioned the final destination of those foremost in faith, the nearest to Him, He next mentioned the end of those on the right — the righteous believers. Maymūn bin Mihrān said that those on the right are lesser in rank than the foremost in faith. So this is not the highest station in Paradise; it is the wide, generous middle of it.

**How wide?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something that should steady any anxious heart. The people of the right are, in the first place, those mindful of Allah and the righteous believers. But sinful believers will also join them: some through the sheer grace of Allah, others forgiven through the intercession of a prophet or of a friend of Allah. Some sinful believers will be punished for their sins, but after serving that punishment they too will be purified and cleansed of the dross of their sins, after which they will join the people of the right — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it (citing Mazharī), the Fire is not in fact a punishment for such a believer so much as a way of cleansing him from the dross of his sins. The right-hand company is therefore not a narrow elite. It is the destination of everyone who died holding on to faith.

## Why these trees?

Before looking at the words one by one, it is worth noticing why these particular images were chosen — and here Mujāhid supplies the key. Commenting on the word *manḍūd*, he said that its fruits are piled on top of each other, and added: **Allah is reminding the Quraysh of these kinds of trees, since they used to like the shade that the ṭalḥ and the sidr provided for them.**

That single remark changes how the passage reads. These were trees the first listeners already knew and loved — and Ibn Kathir tells us plainly what the worldly versions were like. The lote tree (*sidr*) of this life is thorny and carries few fruits. The *ṭalḥ*, on one description, was a large thorny shrub that used to grow in the area of Ḥijāz (western Arabia).

So Allah does not describe Paradise with something unimaginable. He reaches for trees His servants already loved, and shows them those trees with their limitations lifted.

## Ayah 28: *sidrin makhḍūd* — the tree with its thorns taken away

**"Amid thornless lote trees."** *Makhḍūd* describes something that has been done *to* the tree. Two explanations are transmitted, and Ibn Kathir accepts both.

The first is the reading of the majority. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Ibn al-Aḥwaṣ, Qasāmah bin Zuhayr, aṣ-Ṣafr bin Nuṣayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ʿAbdullāh bin Kathīr, as-Suddī, Abū Ḥazrah and several others said it means **the kind without thorns.**

The second is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and likewise from ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid and Qatādah: it is **the tree that is laden with fruits.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives both senses in the same way: *sidr* is the lote tree, and *makhḍūd* means a tree having its thorns removed, and also a tree having its branches bent because of the abundance of its fruit.

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is that there is no need to choose: it is the one with a full load of fruits and without thorns, so both meanings apply. And notice the elegance of that. In this life the lote tree is thorny and carries few fruits; in the Hereafter, Ibn Kathir says, it is the opposite — no thorns, and plenty of fruit, the weight of which strains its trunk. The two halves of the word answer the two disappointments of the worldly tree.

**The scale of it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that, unlike the lote trees of this world, the fruits of the heavenly lote trees will be as large as clay jugs, and their taste cannot be compared to anything found here — a description it attributes to a hadith without naming a collection, so we take the picture without attaching it to one.

**Thorns turned into fruit.** ʿUtbah bin ʿAbd as-Sulamī related that he was sitting with Allah's Messenger ﷺ when a bedouin came and asked about the tree in Paradise that has more thorns than any other — meaning the *ṭalḥ*. The Prophet ﷺ answered that for each spot where there had been a thorn on it, Allah instead put fruit, a food having seventy colours, each one different from the other. (Ibn Kathir does not name a collection for this report, so we take the teaching without attributing it to one.) It is a striking way of putting it: in Paradise the very points where a thing used to hurt you become the points where it feeds you.

## Ayah 29: *ṭalḥin manḍūd* — fruit stacked in layers

**"Clusters of bananas."** Here the classical commentary genuinely divides, and it is worth reporting the disagreement rather than flattening it.

On one explanation, mentioned by Ibn Kathir, *ṭalḥ* refers to the large thorny shrub that used to grow in the area of Ḥijāz.

On the other, transmitted far more widely among the early authorities, *ṭalḥ* is **the banana tree**. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this from Abū Saʿīd, and said that the like is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Qasāmah bin Zuhayr, Qatādah and Abū Ḥazrah. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said similarly, and Ibn Zayd added the linguistic detail that settles it for many: **the people of Yemen call the banana tree *ṭalḥ***. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Jarīr mentioned no other explanation for *ṭalḥ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the same view.

**Manḍūd** is the word that makes the image work. Mujāhid explained it as meaning that its fruits are piled on top of each other. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "the trees of *ṭalḥ*, having layers one upon the other," and glosses *manḍūd* as "clustered" — fruits piled on top of each other as in a bunch of bananas. If you have ever looked closely at a banana bunch, you have seen *manḍūd*: tier upon tier, the whole stem furred with fruit from top to bottom, nothing wasted, no gap.

So ayah 28 gives you a tree whose branches bend under their own harvest, and ayah 29 gives you fruit arranged in dense, ordered layers. Abundance in the first, and in the second abundance that is not chaotic but beautifully stacked.

## Ayah 30: *ẓillin mamdūd* — shade drawn out without end

**"Extended shade."** Ibn Kathir glosses *mamdūd* simply as "extended"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "a shade, spread all over."

What makes this ayah unforgettable is that the Prophet ﷺ himself attached a hadith to it and told his Companions to read it. Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"In Paradise, there is a tree that a rider can travel for a hundred years under its shade but would not be able to pass it"** — and then said, *"Recite if you will: 'And in shade extended.'"* Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim also collected this hadith; Imām Aḥmad recorded it from Abū Hurayrah with nearly the same wording, and Muslim, al-Bukhārī and ʿAbdur-Razzāq collected it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from the Ṣaḥīḥain — that is, the two collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim — in the same terms.

Take that measure seriously. Not a hundred years to reach the tree — a hundred years riding *under the shadow of one tree*, and still not past it. The Arabic word is not "vast" or "cool"; it is "extended", and the hadith tells you what that extension means.

## Holding the three together

Read ayat 28–30 as one movement and their logic appears. What they promise, in order, is:

- **What harms you is removed.** The thorn is taken off the branch (ayah 28).
- **What nourishes you is multiplied.** The fruit is heaped in layers, the branch bent with it (ayat 28–29).
- **What shelters you never runs out.** The shade is extended beyond the reach of a hundred years' riding (ayah 30).

That is a complete account of ease. The worldly lote tree, as Ibn Kathir describes it, fails on the first two counts at once: it wounds you, and it gives you little. The people of the right are given the same familiar goods with those failures taken out of them, and the shade given without limit.

## Living it

**Let the description do its work as longing.** Mujāhid's point is that Allah is reminding the Quraysh of trees whose shade they already loved. Allah reaches for what His servants already know and love, and shows them its perfected form. The right response is not analysis but desire.

**Notice how the Prophet ﷺ handled a blunt question.** A bedouin came asking about the thorniest tree in Paradise, and he ﷺ did not scold him for so earthy a question; he answered it, and turned the thorn itself into the promise.

**Recite the ayah when you remember the tree.** "Recite if you will: *And in shade extended.*" The Prophet ﷺ tied the report to the verse deliberately. Reading ayah 30 is meant to summon that hundred-year shadow, not merely to pass over two Arabic words.

**And do not despair of the right hand.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's note on ayah 27 is the pastoral heart of the passage: the people of the right include not only those mindful of Allah but the forgiven, the interceded-for, and even the believer who is purified first and admitted after. Aim higher than that station if you can — but know that the door to it is wider than your own record.

passages.title: Flowing water, unfailing fruit, raised couches
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are one continuous scene: the garden promised to the Companions of the Right, described through water, fruit, the permanence of that fruit, and the place where they recline. What holds them together is a single idea running underneath the imagery — everything that spoils a garden in this world has been taken out of that one.

## Where we are in the surah

Ibn Kathir explains that after Allah described the final destination of those foremost in faith, the nearest to Him, He turned to the end of those on the right — the righteous believers. Maymun bin Mihran said that those on the right are lesser in rank than the foremost in faith. So this is not the highest tier of Paradise being described here; it is the reward of ordinary sincere believers, and it is already overwhelming.

The description opens in ayah 27 with a question that is really an exclamation — *and those on the right, how (fortunate) will be those on the right?* Ibn Kathir reads it as: who are they, what is their condition, what will their destination be like? Ayat 28 onward are Allah's own answer, and our passage sits in the middle of it.

The scene just before ours (ayat 28–30) is trees: *sidr makhdud* — the lote tree stripped of thorns and heavy with fruit — and *talh mandud*, whose fruits, said Mujahid, are piled one above the other, under shade that stretches on. Mujahid also noted that Allah is reminding the Quraysh of exactly these trees, because they loved the shade the *talh* and *sidr* gave them. The address begins with what the listener already loves. Then, from ayah 31, it moves to water.

## Ayah 31 — water flowing constantly

**وَمَاءٍ مَّسْكُوبٍ** — *and water, poured forth.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sense of this in a single line: the water will be flowing constantly on the surface of the ground.

Two words in that line carry the whole promise. *Constantly* — it does not stop, and there is no point at which it fails. *On the surface of the ground* — it is simply there, in the open, in front of them.

Notice where the description of the Garden chooses to begin: not with some marvel, but with the plainest necessity there is — and even that is given without limit and without interruption.

## Ayah 32 — fruit in abundance

**وَفَاكِهَةٍ كَثِيرَةٍ** — *and abundant fruit.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two senses in *kathīrah*, "abounding": first, that there will be a great quantity of fruit; second, that there will be an uncountable variety and number of kinds. Abundance in Paradise is not a mountain of the same thing. It is endless quantity *and* endless difference.

Ibn Kathir says the ayah indicates plenty of fruits of various kinds — such as no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard of, and no heart has ever imagined. He connects it to Allah's words about the people of the Garden: *Every time they will be provided with a fruit therefrom, they will say: "This is what we were provided with before," and they will be given things in resemblance* (2:25). His comment on that is worth pausing over: **the shape will appear similar, but the taste is different.** Familiarity without repetition — you recognise it, and it is still new.

## Ayah 33 — the two things that end a pleasure

**لَّا مَقْطُوعَةٍ وَلَا مَمْنُوعَةٍ** — *never cut off, never withheld.*

This is the hinge of the passage. Having named the fruit, Allah removes the two things that in this world always end our enjoyment of fruit: time, and permission.

**Not *maqṭūʿah* — the season never ends.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *maqṭūʿah* means fruit whose supply is cut off at the end of the season. In this world most fruits are seasonal: some bear in summer, some in winter, some in the rainy season — and once the season of the fruit is over, it ceases to be available. The fruits of Paradise never run out in any season; they will always be available for those who want to eat from them. Ibn Kathir says the same: their supply never runs out, winter or summer; they are always there for whoever wants to eat, forever.

**Not *mamnūʿah* — no one stands between you and it.** Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a strikingly concrete picture: in this world there are caretakers appointed to look after the gardens, who stop people and forbid them from picking the fruit. In the gardens of Paradise there will be no such hindrance; its people will be able to pick whenever they wish. Every one of us has stood outside a wall looking at fruit that was not ours. That experience does not exist there.

Ibn Kathir adds that whenever these fruits are desired they will be available and easy to grasp by Allah's power, and he quotes Qatadah: *"Nothing will prevent them from reaching out to get these fruits — no branches, thorns or distance."* Read that list back against ayah 28: the lote tree of this world is thorny and carries few fruits; in the Hereafter it is the reverse — no thorns, and so much fruit that the weight strains the trunk. The thorn is gone, the branch does not fend off the hand, and nothing is out of reach. Ibn Kathir also recalls a report mentioned earlier in his commentary, that whenever someone takes a fruit in Paradise, another one grows in its place.

So *lā maqṭūʿah wa lā mamnūʿah* is not decorative repetition. One negation abolishes scarcity in time; the other abolishes scarcity in access.

## What the Sunnah shows us of that fruit

Around these ayat Ibn Kathir gathers several hadith that let us feel the scale of what is being described.

**The size of the fruit.** In the Two Sahihs, Sidrat al-Muntaha — the tree in the seventh heaven — is described with leaves like the ears of elephants and fruits resembling the clay jugs of Hajar.

**A cluster he almost brought back.** The Two Sahihs also record from Ibn 'Abbas that the sun was eclipsed and Allah's Messenger ﷺ led the people in the Eclipse prayer. Afterwards they said, "O Allah's Messenger, we saw you reach out for something while standing, but then you stepped back." He said: *"I saw Paradise and reached out for a cluster of fruit from it. Had I done so, you would have kept eating from it for the remainder of the life of the world."* One cluster; the whole world eating from it until the world ends. That is the Prophet's ﷺ own commentary on *fruit in plenty, never cut off.*

**The bedouin and the tree called Tuba.** Imam Ahmad recorded from 'Utbah bin 'Abd As-Sulami that a bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him about Paradise. He asked, "Does Paradise have fruits?" The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Yes, and it also has a tree called Tuba."* The bedouin asked whether it looked like any of the trees that grow in his own area. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"There is nothing resembling it among the trees in your land."* Then he ﷺ asked the man whether he had travelled to Ash-Sham. He had not. The Prophet ﷺ told him it looks like a tree that grows in Ash-Sham called *Al-Jawzah*, which stands on one stem but whose branches grow all around to the fullest extent.

The bedouin kept asking, and every answer came in the currency of his own life. How big is the cluster of its fruits? *"The distance that the crow flies in one month without rest."* How huge is its trunk? *"If a four-year-old she-camel that your family owns travels it, it will not completely pass its trunk until its shoulders break from old age."* Does it bear grapes? Yes. How big are the grapes? The Prophet ﷺ asked him: has your father ever slaughtered a ram, then skinned it and given the skin to your mother, asking her to make a hanging bucket out of it? The man said yes — and then said it himself: "This grape would suffice for me and my family!" The Prophet ﷺ agreed: *"Yes, and also for the rest of your clan."*

Look at how that teaching works. The bedouin is handed no abstractions; he is walked from a leather bucket in his mother's hands to a single grape of Paradise, and arrives at the conclusion himself. It is the same method as the ayat: *sidr*, *talh*, shade, flowing water, fruit — familiar things, stretched until they break open into what no eye has seen.

## Ayah 34 — couches raised high

**وَفُرُشٍ مَّرْفُوعَةٍ** — *and elevated furnishings.*

Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: high, soft and comfortable. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the words up. *Furush* is the plural of *firāsh*, which means a bed, a couch, a mattress. *Marfūʿah* lexically means "upraised, elevated". Why raised? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers three possibilities: because the place itself is high; or because the mattresses will not be on the ground but upon thrones or beds; or because the couches themselves will be thick, and so of high quality.

Here the scholars genuinely differ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that **some exegetes take *furush* in the sense of women**, since that is one of the meanings of *firāsh* — as in the Prophetic tradition *al-walad lil-firāsh*, "the child belongs to the *firāsh*," where *firāsh* refers to the wife. On that reading *marfūʿah* would mean "high-ranking" rather than physically raised. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is corroborated by the characteristics of the women of Paradise described in the verses that follow.

Ibn Kathir reaches the same connection from the side of Arabic style. He observes that the ayat which follow — *Verily, We have created them a special creation, and made them virgins…* — describe the women who will be on the beds and couches, yet they are not directly mentioned: the mention of the beds is itself the hint. He gives a parallel from elsewhere in the Qur'an: of Sulaymān and the horses displayed before him, Allah says *till the time was over, and it had hidden in the veil* (38:31–32), where "it" refers to the sun setting, according to the scholars of tafsir. Al-Akhfash said that *Verily, We have created them* implies the maidens of Paradise although it did not mention them directly; Abu 'Ubaydah said that they had been mentioned before, in *And Hur with wide lovely eyes, like preserved pearls* (56:22–23).

Either way — whether ayah 34 speaks of the bedding, or on the second reading of the companions upon it — this is the last brushstroke of the scene. Water flows, fruit hangs within reach, and the believer is at rest, raised up.

## Living it

Notice what Allah chose to promise. Not one exotic marvel, but water that never stops flowing, and then the removal of every frustration attached to ordinary good things: fruit that has a season, a garden with a caretaker who forbids the picking, a thorn on the branch, a distance between the hand and what it wants, a resting place on the ground. The Garden is described as this life with its griefs subtracted and its goods multiplied without limit.

Two things follow. First, read slowly, these ayat shrink the pleasures we chase here to their true size — every one of them is cut off by a season and fenced off by someone. Wanting the unending thing is the sane response. Second, this is the portion of the Companions of the Right, believers whom Maymun bin Mihran placed below the foremost in rank. If this is the lower of the two portions this surah describes, no believer has cause to despair of Allah's generosity — and none has cause to settle for it either.

passages.title: Mates created anew for the people of the right
passages.tafsir:
This passage closes the portrait of **the people of the right** (*aṣḥāb al-yamīn*) — the righteous believers whose reward Allah describes after He has finished describing those foremost in faith, the nearest to Him. Ibn Kathir notes that Maymun bin Mihran said the people of the right are lesser in rank than the foremost; yet look at what "lesser" means here. Ayat 35–38 describe the companions Allah creates for them, and ayat 39–40 tell us how many will receive this: crowds from the earliest generations and crowds from the last.

## The pronoun with no visible owner

The passage opens with a puzzle. Ayah 35 says **"Indeed, We have created *them* anew"** — *innā anshaʾnāhunna inshāʾan* — but the "them" (*hunna*, a feminine plural pronoun) has no noun before it in the immediately preceding ayat. Who are "they"?

The commentators give three complementary answers:

- **Ibn Kathir**: these ayat describe the women who will be on the beds and couches of ayah 34, and because mentioning the beds already hints at them, they were not directly mentioned. He gives a parallel from elsewhere in the Qur'an: when Sulayman's story mentions the well-trained horses displayed before him and then says "till the time was over, and *it* had hidden in the veil" (38:31–32), the scholars of tafsir take "it" to be the setting sun — named by nothing but the evening itself.
- **Al-Akhfash** said ayah 35 implies the maidens of Paradise although it does not mention them directly.
- **Abu ʿUbaydah** said they were already mentioned earlier in the sūrah, in "And *ḥūr* with wide lovely eyes, like preserved pearls" (56:22–23).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gathers the same threads: the pronoun refers to the women of Paradise, mentioned in the more distant ayat 22–23; and if *firāsh* in ayah 34 itself refers to the women of Paradise, then the pronoun's antecedent is quite obvious. Either way, the mention of beds, couches and thrones supplies the context.

There is a lesson in the very indirectness. The Qur'an speaks of intimacy with a veil of allusion, naming the setting rather than the persons.

## "Created anew" — what *inshāʾ* means

*Inshāʾ*, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, simply means **to create**. But the ayah does not say "We created them"; it says "We created them *a creating*" — repeating the verbal noun after the verb, which is why translators reach for words like "perfectly created", and why Ibn Kathir renders it "a special creation". The doubling insists: this is not a continuation of anything that came before. It is a fresh making.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān unpacks that fresh making in two directions:

1. **The ḥūr of Paradise are created without being born biologically.** They have no infancy, no lineage, no growing up. They are created in a special way.
2. **The women of this world who enter Paradise will be reshaped.** Those who were ugly, dark-coloured or old in this life will be made beautiful, young and graceful.

Ibn Kathir says the same of ayah 35: it means that **in the other life, after they became old in this life, they are brought back virgin, youthful, delightfully passionate with their husbands, beautiful, kind and cheerful.**

Read that slowly, because it is one of the most merciful sentences in the whole description of Paradise. The believing woman who spent her years in worship and service, whose body wore out with age, who watched her beauty leave her in the mirror — she is not carried into Paradise as a ruin to be pitied. She is **created anew**.

## The old woman who wept

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records two narrations here that make the point unforgettable.

It is recorded in **Tirmidhi and Baihaqi**, on the authority of Sayyidnā Anas, that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said in explanation of ayah 35 that the women who in this world were old, blear-eyed, grey-haired and of ugly features will be made beautiful and young in this new creation.

And **Baihaqi** also reports from Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that an old lady asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to pray to Allah that she may enter Paradise. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, in a humorous way, *lā tadkhulu l-jannatu ʿajūz* — "Old ladies will not enter Paradise." Hearing this the old lady got very sad, and according to some narrations began to weep. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then explained that she would not be **old** when she entered it — she would be transformed into a young, beautiful woman. And then he recited this very ayah. (Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites this from Mazharī.)

That is the tone of the passage. A moment of humour from the Prophet ﷺ, a moment of tears, and then a verse of the Qur'an handed to an old woman as her personal consolation.

## Ayah 36: *abkāran*

**"Making them virgins."** *Abkār*, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes, is the plural of *bikr*, "virgin". The sense given there is that the creation of the maidens of Paradise is of such a nature that they remain like virgins however often husband and wife are together. The freshness of the first meeting is never spent. Nothing in Paradise wears out — not the fruit of ayat 32–33, whose supply, Ibn Kathir says, never runs out, winter or summer, and not this.

Ibn Kathir relates here what the sources report of the believer's capacity in Paradise. **Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi** recorded from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the believer will be given such-and-such strength for women; when Anas asked whether one would be able to do that, he ﷺ said, "He will be given the strength of a hundred (men)." **At-Tirmidhi** also recorded it and said, "Ṣaḥīḥ Gharīb." **Abu Al-Qasim At-Tabarani** recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked whether the people of Paradise will have relations with their wives there, and he ﷺ answered in terms of a like abundance. Of this report **Al-Hafiz Abu ʿAbdullah Al-Maqdisi** said, "In my view, this Hadith meets the criteria of the Ṣaḥīḥ, and Allah knows best."

The point is not appetite. It is that in Paradise the body is no longer the limiting thing it is here — the frailty and decline that shadow every earthly pleasure are simply gone.

## Ayah 37: *ʿuruban atrāban* — loving, and of one age

Two single words, and the whole emotional character of Paradise is in them.

**ʿUrub** (singular *ʿarūbah*) is defined in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān as *a woman who loves her husband passionately and is his beloved* — note that it runs both ways. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, through Saʿid bin Jubayr, that they are in an infatuated state with their husbands; and Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said, **"The Urub and their husbands are their sweet hearts, and they are their husbands' sweet hearts."** Ibn Kathir adds that similar was said by ʿAbdullah bin Sarjis, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Yahya bin Abi Kathir, ʿAtiyah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others.

So the reward is not merely a beautiful companion. It is **mutual love**: to be desired by the one you desire. Anyone who has seen a marriage of mismatched affection understands what a mercy that is.

**Atrāb** (singular *tirb*) is the more evocative word. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives its root sense precisely: *a person of equal age who played together with his mate in dust*. It is a childhood word — the friend you grew up beside, whose years match yours exactly. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, through Ad-Dahhak, that *atrāb* means "they will be of one age, thirty-three years old"; Mujahid said "equal (age)", and in another narration "similar (age)"; ʿAtiyah said "comparative". Maʿārif ul Qurʾān concludes that men and women will be made of equal ages in Paradise, some narrations reporting that they will be about thirty-three years old.

Put the two words together and you have a description no earthly marriage fully achieves: **love returned in equal measure, between two people who never grow apart in age.** There is no ageing, and therefore no one left behind.

## Ayah 38: "for the people of the right"

Ibn Kathir gives two readings of *li-aṣḥāb al-yamīn*, and it is worth keeping both:

- **Ibn Jarir's view**, which Ibn Kathir says appears to be the meaning: these women were **created for** the people of the right — created, kept, or given to them in marriage. The whole sequence, ayat 35–38, reads as one statement: We created them a special creation, made them virgins, *ʿurub*, *atrāb* — *for those on the right*.
- **A second possibility**: that the phrase attaches to the description just before it, *atrāban*, meaning they are of one age **with** the people of the right.

Here Ibn Kathir brings the description recorded by **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** from Abu Hurayrah: the first group to enter Paradise will be shining like the moon when it is full, and the next group like the most radiant planet in the sky; they will not urinate, relieve nature, spit or blow their noses; their combs will be of gold and their sweat of musk, and censers of aloeswood will be used; their wives will be from *Al-Ḥūr Al-ʿAyn*; their shape will be similar to each other, the shape of their father Adam, sixty cubits high in the sky.

Notice that the description does not stop at the companions. The people entering Paradise are themselves described as utterly changed — free of every indignity the body imposes here.

## Ayat 39–40: how many

**"A multitude from the earlier generations, and a multitude from the later generations."** The word is *thullah* — rendered "a multitude", "a large party". Ibn Kathir's plain reading: a multitude of those on the right will come from the earlier generations and a multitude from the later generations.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān points out that the same pair of phrases appeared earlier in the sūrah regarding *the foremost*, where the commentators offered two views of who "the earlier" and "the later" are:

- If **"the earlier"** means the generations from Adam (peace be upon him) to the period just before the advent of the Prophet ﷺ, and **"the later"** means the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ until the Day of Judgment — as some commentators have opined — then the ayat mean this: one large party of the people of the right drawn from *all* previous communities combined, and another large party from this Ummah **alone**. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān calls that a great honour — that a community which lived so short a period in this world could be compared to all the previous communities, who were headed by hundreds of thousands of Prophets (peace be upon them). And the wording "many from the later generations" leaves scope for that party to be the larger of the two.
- If instead **both** groups are taken from within this Ummah, then even the later generations of this Ummah will not be totally deprived of the foremost, though their number will be less; while the people of the right will be large in number in both the earlier and the later generations.
